title: Watch the clouds

segments.voice: Yesterday, the night sky and the Pleiades. Your line was the nearest stars. This week: awe walks, more time, tall trees, moral beauty, a sunrise, the stars. Science first, then practice. Today the week ends with an awe that's easy to find.

A child lies on the grass and says, that one's a dragon. A minute later the dragon has lost its head and become a boat. A minute after that, the boat is coming apart into something with no name at all. Somewhere along the way, the game stops, and clouds turn into weather: will it rain, do I need a jacket? But the show never stopped. Right now, over every rooftop, shapes are forming that have never been seen before and won't be seen again. Clouds never repeat.
screen: `A DRAGON, THEN A BOAT.` → `CLOUDS BECOME WEATHER.` → `SHAPES THAT NEVER RETURN.`

segments.voice: First, what a cloud is. Not a thing, really. An event. Water rises as vapor, cools, and gathers into countless tiny drops on specks of dust, and the cloud is the shape that water takes for a while before it changes again. It's always being made and unmade at once, which is why no two are ever the same. Second, an old line that watched the same cycle. Ecclesiastes, in the King James words: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again." The writer saw water going round and round, and a cloud is that water on its way back up. Third, a philosopher who built a whole teaching on change. Heraclitus, the ancient Greek thinker, is remembered, through later writers, for saying you can't step into the same river twice. A later summary of his teaching boiled it down to two Greek words: panta rhei, everything flows. Fourth, why watching clouds is a practice of awe. It's free. It needs no travel and no alarm. And it trains the eye on something that won't hold still for you. The cloud you're looking at is never the same as it was a breath ago. Neither, if you look closely, is the one looking.
screen: `A CLOUD IS AN EVENT, NOT A THING.` · `ALL THE RIVERS RUN INTO THE SEA.` · `PANTA RHEI: EVERYTHING FLOWS.` · `FREE, AND IT WON'T HOLD STILL.` · then, large: `NEVER THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Find a window with some sky in it, or step outside, and pick one cloud, or a patch of blue to wait in if the sky is clear. Watch one edge without naming the shape; when it becomes something else or thins away, let it. Breathe slowly, and let your attention move as slowly as the cloud does.
Panta rhei. Heraclitus's two Greek words for everything flows, the teaching behind watching clouds that form, change and never return. Today's word.
Your line: never the same. Somewhere overhead, a dragon is already becoming a boat. That's the week, and day one thousand thirty-six.

howItsDone: Cloud watchers lie down or sit where they can see a wide stretch of sky and follow the clouds as they form and change, without hurrying and often without naming the shapes.

chat.says: What does 'panta rhei' have to do with watching clouds?
options: It means everything flows: like a cloud, nothing holds still, not even the one watching.
It means look up: Heraclitus taught people to read the weather in the clouds.
It means fast weather: clouds move quicker than anything else in the sky.
chat.meaning: Panta rhei, everything flows, is a later summary of Heraclitus's teaching on change. A cloud is always being made and unmade, never the same twice.
